Title: The Current State of 3D-Printed Prostheses Clinical Outcomes: A Systematic Review[1]
Method: Methods reported include 3D scanning and digital design workflows, 3D printing/additive manufacturing, photograph-based distance measurements with ImageJ scaling, manual anthropometry (tape measure, skinfold caliper, goniometer), CAD/3D modeling, and comparative analysis of digitally versus manually designed sockets[1]
Product Type: Upper-limb prostheses (3D-printed hands, wrist-driven and myoelectric devices) and lower-limb prostheses (including sockets and amphibious designs)[1]
Population: Combined sample across included studies: 177 participants (various ages and amputation levels reported in individual studies, e.g., trans-radial, partial hand, trans-tibial)[1]
Measurements Used: Measurements used include photograph-based linear measurements calibrated with a ruler, direct anthropometry (circumferences, skinfolds), range of motion, strength testing, socket geometric measures (volume, height) and patient-reported Socket Comfort Scores[1]
Study Design: Systematic review summarizing included primary studies of mixed designs: cross-sectional, prospective cohort, comparative, observational, pilot and feasibility studies[1]
Key Findings: 3D-printed prostheses can enhance personalization, fit, comfort, and satisfaction; digital/photograph-based sizing can be accurate and enable remote fitting; digital sockets differ geometrically from manual casts and are often preferred by users, but evidence is limited by small sample sizes and variable quality[1]
Journal Source: Journal of Functional Biomaterials (J. Funct. Biomater.) [1]
Quality Level: Overall evidence quality: Mostly moderate/low (majority rated 'fair'; one 'good'; one 'poor')[1]

Title: Antropometric Based Optimization Of Wheelchair Design For Enhanced User Ergonomics[2]
Method: Anthropometric data collection and analysis using manual anthropometry (implied), with statistical analysis including data normality test, data uniformity test, data sufficiency test, and percentile calculation to determine design criteria[2]
Population: Elderly wheelchair users; sample size and age range not specified in source. The study reports significant variation in anthropometric dimensions among users[2]
Measurements Used: Seat width, backrest height, footrest position; specific anthropometric landmarks or exact measurements not provided in text[2]
Study Design: Observational study with anthropometric data collection and statistical analysis to derive percentile-based design criteria (procedure described in methods)[2]
Key Findings: Anthropometric-based adjustments (seat width, backrest height, footrest) produced prototype improvements in pressure distribution and sitting posture and yielded design criteria better matching elderly ergonomic needs[2]
Journal Source: Universitas Ahmad Dahlan Public Health Conference Proceeding[2]
Quality Level: Moderate: study applies statistical anthropometric analysis and prototype testing with reported improvements, but full details on sample size and experimental rigour are not provided in the source text[2]

Title: Topologically Optimized Anthropomorphic Prosthetic Limb: Finite Element Analysis and Mechanical Evaluation Using Plantogram-Derived Foot Pressure Data[3]
Method: 3D scanning of an actual foot using an Artec Eva scanner; use of plantogram-derived foot pressure data to set boundary/loading conditions; Finite Element Analysis (explicit dynamics) for static and dynamic simulation and topology optimization; fabrication/testing of TPMS gyroid lattice specimens via SLS additive manufacturing and mechanical compression/loading-unloading tests to measure energy absorption and damping[3]
Population: Plantogram data from a single male basketball athlete (75 kg) used for loading conditions; informed consent obtained[3]
Measurements Used: Plantogram foot pressure contours and derived regional dimensions (metatarsal, calcaneus) for ROI and loading; stress values from plantogram (pressure) and FEA stress/strain outputs; 3D scan geometry of a male foot to derive anthropomorphic shape[3]
Study Design: Experimental/engineering study combining computational FEA simulations and laboratory mechanical testing of fabricated specimens informed by empirical plantogram data[3]
Key Findings: A gyroid TPMS anthropomorphic prosthetic foot (40% relative density) matched plantogram-derived loading and showed unified stress distribution; TPU-GTR composite with gyroid lattice provided adequate energy absorption and damping (loss factor ~0.18) suitable for dynamic loads; minimum functional relative density estimated ~33% from scaling laws[3]
Quality Level: Moderate: engineering experimental study with FEA and lab tests supporting design decisions, but limited external validity due to use of plantogram data from a single athlete and no shared datasets[3]

Title: Applying 3D Scanning and Printing Techniques to Produce Upper Limb Prostheses: Bibliometric Analysis and Scoping Review[4]
Method: Uses 3D scanning and 3D printing workflows: surface capture with commercial 3D scanners, CT scanning, and photogrammetry to collect geometry; CAD/model adjustment and 3D printing (FDM, SLS, SLA) for fabrication; bibliometric and qualitative analysis of methods across studies[4]
Population: Studies synthesized from literature (n=274 papers); populations across included studies vary and include patients, children, and people with upper-limb deficiency but specific sample sizes per study are not provided in this source[4]
Measurements Used: Body geometry capture (external surface meshes) via CT, commercial optical 3D scanners, and photogrammetry; measurements for socket/shape/size, and parameters for scaling/parameterizing open-source designs. Specific anthropometric landmarks/dimensions not enumerated in this source[4]
Study Design: Scoping review (bibliometric analysis and qualitative synthesis) of published literature following PRISMA-ScR[4]
Key Findings: 3D scanning/printing enable faster, more customizable, and lower-cost production of upper-limb prostheses; trends include increased use of scanners, focus on finger mechanisms, control/sensing advances, and accessibility via open-source designs. Scanning methods (CT, optical scanners, photogrammetry) offer alternatives to casting but have limitations capturing nuanced features affecting fit[4]
Journal Source: MDPI (proceedings/journal PDF provided) — full citation not explicitly stated in source; original PDF URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-1592/7/2/26/pdf?version=1740996517[4]
Quality Level: Moderate: systematic scoping review with large literature inclusion (n=274) and PRISMA-ScR methods, but limitations include heterogeneity of included studies, variable reporting of primary-study methods, and exclusion of non-English and proprietary sources[4]

Title: Methods to assess lower limb prosthetic adaptation: a systematic review[5]
Method: Predominant methods reported: mobility evaluation, gait analysis, measurement of physical variables, and stability assessment (including functional tests and self-report questionnaires)[5]
Population: Studies of people with lower limb amputation (various samples aggregated in review); specific sample sizes vary by included study — review covers studies published 2011–2023[5]
Measurements Used: Measurements include residual limb characterization and interface/socket variables, mobility and functional test scores, gait parameters, and physical variables related to stump/socket interface[5]
Key Findings: Mobility evaluation is the primary predictor of prosthetic fitting; functional tests and self-report questionnaires are the most widely used methods; laboratory-specific methods for measuring specific variables are less implemented in clinical practice and should be adapted for clinical use[5]
Journal Source: Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation (J Neuroeng Rehabil)[5]
Quality Level: Moderate (systematic review synthesizing multiple studies; quality depends on included studies—review methodology reported but primary-study heterogeneity limits strength)[5]

Title: METHOD FOR CREATING A DIGITAL ATLAS OF 3D MODELS OF HUMAN ANATOMY FOR PROSTHETICS[6]
Method: Describes automated digital methods: conversion of DICOM (DCM) CT/MRI scans and 3D scans to 3D models using Python scripts and PyVista, file-format unification (STL/OBJ/BLEND), text-based model search and API-driven requests for model adaptation and export for 3D printing[6]
Product Type: Prosthetic devices (reference limb models, prosthetic limbs, implants)[6]
Measurements Used: Specifies storage and use of 3D anatomical characteristics and models derived from CT/MRI DICOM data and 3D scans (mesh formats STL/OBJ), but does not list specific anthropometric landmarks or numerical body dimensions[6]
Study Design: Methodological/technical development paper describing a system and proposed methodology (development study)[6]
Key Findings: Presents that an integrated digital atlas and automated conversion pipeline can improve 3D reconstruction accuracy, simplify prosthesis design workflows, enable adaptation of reference models to individual anatomy, and streamline export for 3D printing and clinical use[6]
Journal Source: Pratsi (institutional/technical journal) — PDF available from pratsi.op.edu.ua[6]
Quality Level: Moderate — technical/method development paper describing system architecture and implementation; lacks reported empirical validation on sample populations or quantitative user studies[6]

Title: EVALUATION OF OFFICE CHAIR DESIGN FROM ERGONOMIC AND ANTHROPOMETRIC PERSPECTIVES[7]
Method: Collected seated anthropometry (11 parameters) and subjective Nordic Body Map questionnaire; statistical analysis including normality tests and percentile calculations (P50/P95) to perform mismatch analysis and percentile-based redesign of chair dimensions[7]
Population: 32 employees (16 men, 16 women), age 24–42 years, employees of Politeknik Industri Furnitur dan Pengolahan Kayu Kendal[7]
Measurements Used: Seated anthropometric measures: popliteal height; buttock-popliteal length; shoulder width; hip width; shoulder height; eye height; seated erect height; seat-to-knee height; buttock-to-knee length; buttock-to-elbow height; backrest inclination angle. Used biomechanical ratios (e.g., seat height vs. popliteal height, seat depth vs. buttock-popliteal length) for mismatch criteria[7]
Study Design: Observational ergonomic study combining cross-sectional anthropometric measurements and questionnaire-based discomfort assessment; followed by design redesign (applied ergonomics) using percentile-based analysis[7]
Key Findings: Found severe anthropometric mismatch (seat height 100%; seat depth 94% men, 88% women) and recommended redesign reducing seat height by 30 mm and seat depth by 66 mm; redesigned dimensions align with national and international ergonomic standards, expected to reduce discomfort[7]
Journal Source: E-Journal of Ganesha Technopolis (?) — source is an e-journal entry available at the provided URL. Title and repository given in source metadata[7]
Quality Level: Moderate — observational study with a small sample (n=32) using systematic anthropometric methods and applied redesign; limited by sample size and lack of extensive usability validation[7]

Title: Evaluation of Office Chairs to Enhance Comfort and Reduce Musculoskeletal Risk in Sedentary Work Environments[8]
Method: Used workforce-specific anthropometric measurements (seat height, seat depth, backrest height, armrest positioning) to redesign chair dimensions; evaluated application with observational ROSA assessments and statistical analysis (paired-sample t-test) to assess ergonomic impact[8]
Population: Polytechnic employees; sample size N=32; age 17–61 years; mixed gender (60% female); heights 155–185 cm[8]
Measurements Used: Anthropometric dimensions: seat height (popliteal height), seat depth, backrest height (shoulder height), armrest positioning; demographic measures: height, weight, BMI[8]
Study Design: Mixed-methods observational intervention (pre-post within-subject trial) with quantitative ROSA assessments, surveys/interviews, and paired-sample t-test analysis[8]
Key Findings: Redesigned chair based on anthropometric data significantly reduced ergonomic risk (ROSA mean 7.03 -> 5.19; mean difference 1.84; paired t-test T=-9.98, p=0.000). Authors note dimensional changes improve fit but recommend adding adjustable features for broader accommodation[8]
Journal Source: Journal with e-ISSN 2714-7010, Vol.6 No.2, April 2025[8]
Quality Level: Moderate: small sample (N=32) and within-subject pre-post design with objective ROSA measures and statistical testing support findings, but limited generalizability and single-site context[8]

Title: Methods to assess lower limb prosthetic adaptation: a systematic review[9]
Method: Systematic review extracting and synthesizing methods reported across studies: literature search and PRISMA screening, data extraction into categories (variables, instruments, conclusions), and critical appraisal. Reported anthropometric/measurement methods in included studies: manual measurements, residual limb volume measurement and accommodation, 3D scanning, pressure sensors, motion capture, instrumented surfaces, alignment tools, specialized software, questionnaires and functional tests[9]
Product Type: Lower-limb prosthetic devices (transtibial and transfemoral sockets and components)[9]
Population: Studies included varied populations across the literature; the review synthesized 48 papers on residual limb measurements in people with lower-limb amputation (various ages, amputation levels transtibial and transfemoral) and publication dates 2011–2023[9]
Measurements Used: Residual limb measurements: limb volume and shape, distances, interface pressure, socket air pressure, temperature, ground reaction forces, angular momentum; measurement techniques include 3D scanning, optical scanners, pressure sensors, instrumented surfaces, motion capture, and automated socket sizing systems[9]
Study Design: Systematic review (synthesis of 48 included studies spanning experimental, observational, case studies, and technical briefs)[9]
Key Findings: Key findings: mobility and functional tests are the most-used predictors of prosthetic adaptation; questionnaires dominate instruments but are subjective; volume/shape measurements (via 3D scanning/optical scanners) and pressure/force measures provide objective design-relevant data; many tools lack prosthesis-specific validation; recommendation to combine objective measurements with functional and self-report measures and to integrate advanced tools into clinical practice to improve fitting and design implications[9]
Quality Level: Moderate: systematic-review level synthesis but many included studies had small/heterogeneous samples, non-randomized designs, and measurement limitations, reducing overall evidence strength[9]

Title: OpenLimbTT, a transtibial residual limb shape model for prosthetics simulation and design: creating a statistical anatomic model using sparse data[10]
Method: Statistical Shape Model (SSM) construction from MRI/CT volume imaging and segmented surface meshes; mesh registration using non-rigid ICP; size-normalisation to estimated full tibia length; Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract modes of variation; prediction methods: Gappy POD/pseudo-inverse and linear regression to predict internal bone geometry from external skin scans; cross-validation via Leave-One-Out testing[10]
Product Type: Transtibial residual limb / prosthetic socket design and prosthetic limb biomechanics[10]
Population: Primary imaging sources comprised 33 MRI/CT scans combined; core MRI subject set described as 11 transtibial amputee participants, with the final SSM training set reduced to 10 after outlier exclusion; participants varied in amputation causes, age and time since amputation (not fully enumerated)[10]
Measurements Used: Segmented 3D anatomical surface meshes (skin and internal bones: tibia, fibula, patella, distal femur); size normalisation using estimated full tibia length; PCA mode scores quantifying amputation height, soft tissue bulk (slender–bulbous), and regional tissue distribution; quantitative error metrics (RMSE of surface deviations) reported for reconstruction and prediction[10]
Study Design: Methodological/observational study developing and validating a Statistical Shape Model using MRI/CT datasets with Leave-One-Out cross-validation (SSM development and evaluation)[10]
Key Findings: SSM can predict internal bone geometry from external skin scans with median bone-prediction RMSE ≈6.5 mm using linear regression; dominant shape variance is amputation height (~82%) and soft tissue bulk (~7.5%); model reconstruction RMSEs for left-out shapes ranged ~4.8–8.9 mm; provides a shared open-access dataset/model to support prosthetic socket design and simulation[10]
Journal Source: medRxiv preprint (full text available at provided medRxiv URL)[10]
Quality Level: Moderate-to-low: methodological advance but limited by small training dataset (SSM trained on n≈10 after outlier exclusion), validated with LOO cross-validation—useful proof-of-concept but requires larger, more diverse data for high confidence[10]

Title: A New Automatic Process Based on Generative Design for CAD Modeling and Manufacturing of Customized Orthosis[11]
Method: Photogrammetry using a smartphone camera for 3D acquisition, reconstruction with Agisoft Metashape, automatic generative-design CAD modeling (Grasshopper/Rhinoceros), and fabrication via FDM 3D printing; clinician/patient usability testing[11]
Population: Case study of at least one patient (approx. 130 photos of the patient's wrist); clinician evaluation by orthopedist. No formal sample size or age range reported[11]
Measurements Used: 3D surface geometry from photogrammetry capturing wrist/hand shape; derived dimensions (wrist width, finger length/width, palm size); boundary landmarks defined interactively on the 3D mesh[11]
Study Design: Case study / methods development with prototype evaluation (observational, design-methods study)[11]
Key Findings: Generative-design pipeline using smartphone photogrammetry produced clinically usable wrist orthosis prototypes; method is user-friendly for non-experts and reduces need for specialized technicians, but limited clinical testing and unknown accuracy metrics were noted[11]
Quality Level: Low — single case-study / prototype evaluation with limited clinical testing and no reported quantitative accuracy or larger sample validation[11]

Title: Standard Guide for Assessing Fit Accommodation of Exoskeletons for Manufacturers and Designers[12]
Method: Provides recommendations to use anthropometric databases matched to target populations, distinguish static vs dynamic fit, and assess accommodation rates using population percentiles and ROM evaluations[12]
Population: Intended user population for exoskeletons; recommends matching anthropometric datasets to the target population (no specific sample size given)[12]
Measurements Used: Body size and shape measures; example: shoulder breadth in standardized postures; use of anthropometric database dimensions and ROM-related clearances[12]
Study Design: Standards/guide document (consensus standard) rather than primary experimental study[12]
Key Findings: Provides design guidance: use appropriate anthropometric databases, estimate accommodation rates, consider subgroup disaccommodation, provide sizing and adjustment criteria, and evaluate static and dynamic fit to inform design and user instructions[12]
Quality Level: Moderate — consensus standard providing best-practice recommendations; not primary empirical study (no sample size)[12]

Title: Customized Orthosis Design Based on Surface Reconstruction from 3D-Scanned Points[13]
Method: Develops and applies a 3D scan-based surface reconstruction pipeline: point-cloud acquisition (laser/structured-light scanners) and preprocessing, iterative B-Spline curve approximation and B-Spline surface interpolation, and optimization using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm to minimize reconstruction error[13]
Product Type: Orthotic device (customized orthosis for finger and foot parts)[13]
Population: Two scanned human body parts (finger and foot); specific sample size, age range, and participant demographics not mentioned in source[13]
Measurements Used: 3D point-cloud coordinates from laser/structured-light scans; derived geometric landmarks and planar cross-sections used to approximate B‑Spline curves and surfaces; reconstruction quality quantified by MRMS/RMS error metrics[13]
Study Design: Method development with numerical experiments and two case studies (observational/technical case study)[13]
Key Findings: Proposed B‑Spline curve–based reconstruction yields lower reconstruction errors than a prior method and produces accurate surfaces suitable for rapid prototyping of customized orthoses, improving fit and potential patient comfort[13]
Quality Level: Moderate: technical methods and quantitative error metrics with two case studies support validity, but limited sample size and lack of clinical/real-user trials reduce evidence strength[13]

Title: A Review on 3D Scanners Studies for Producing Customized Orthoses[14]
Method: Review of non‑radiative 3D digitization methods for anthropometry: laser scanning, structured light, photogrammetry, and optical scanners; data processing into CAD/mesh, reverse engineering workflows, and additive manufacturing (3D printing) for producing custom orthoses[14]
Product Type: Custom orthoses (foot orthoses, ankle-foot orthoses, spinal orthosis examples discussed)[14]
Population: Varied across included studies; review included human participants in orthotics studies (examples include single-subject AFO studies and clinical users of AFO/FO); specific sample sizes and age ranges are reported per included study in the review rather than as a unified sample in this paper[14]
Measurements Used: 3D point clouds and meshes derived from optical triangulation (surface geometry capture); mesh/mesh processing in CAD for dimensional measurements and model adjustment (no specific anatomical landmark list provided)[14]
Study Design: Systematic review of studies using 3D scanners for custom orthoses (PRISMA-guided)[14]
Key Findings: Photogrammetry highlighted as most suitable for human limb acquisition; 3D scanning+AM enables accurate geometry and improved user satisfaction vs plaster casting; trade-offs include processing time, cost and training barriers for clinical adoption[14]
Quality Level: Moderate — systematic review methodology (PRISMA) synthesizing 20 included studies; quality depends on heterogenous small‑sample primary studies noted by authors[14]

Title: Anatomical-Based Customized Cervical Orthosis Design in Automation[15]
Method: Methods include surface 3D scanning using a handheld scanner (Go!Scan 50) to capture neck geometry[15], automatic anatomical feature identification via a pre-set 12-point template with bipartite graph matching and the Hungarian algorithm for feature matching after distance normalization[15], template normalization/denormalization and coordinate transforms (Cartesian⇔ cylindrical) to map templates to individual scans and generate centerlines and coverage regions for orthosis geometry[15], procedural mesh operations (offsetting, Laplacian smoothing, Boolean ops) to create inner/outer layers and allowances[15], and application of finite element analysis (ANSYS) to assess structural strength and determine minimum thickness requirements[15].
Product Type: Cervical orthosis (custom 3D-printed two-piece rigid neck orthosis)[15]
Population: Not clearly specified sample demographics; study used scanning procedures on subjects (scanning protocol described) and finite element analysis based on one subject model[15].
Measurements Used: Used 3D surface geometry with 0.5 mm resolution and a set of 12 anatomical landmark features (chin, mandibular angles, side neck points, clavicles, sternum, external occipital protuberance, mastoid processes, C7 spinous process) as measurement anchors; coordinate systems and centerlines extracted from scan mesh for dimensional offsets and allowances[15]
Study Design: Design and methods paper with computational development, case-based prototyping and simulation (automated design workflow description + FEA on one-subject model) — observational/development study rather than large-scale experimental trial[15].
Key Findings: Key findings: automated CAD workflow using 3D scans and anatomical-template matching can generate customized cervical orthoses; FEA indicates minimum PLA thickness of ~5 mm for safety at 20% infill; software embeds anatomical landmarks and allowances to improve fit, ventilation and comfort and reduce manual design effort[15]
Quality Level: Moderate-to-low: development and simulation study with detailed methods but limited validation (FEA based on one-subject model, no clinical trial or large sample)[15].

Title: Insights into the spectrum of transtibial prosthetic socket design from expert clinicians and their digital records[16]
Method: Analysis of 3D residual limb and CAD/CAM socket surface meshes from paired scans; alignment using ampscan toolbox and iterative closest point (ICP); manual identification of rectification clusters and quantification of carve/build depths; statistical analyses including Spearman correlations, linear regression, kernel density estimation (KDE) and Gaussian Naïve Bayes classification to interpret associations and predict design patterns[16]
Population: 134 individuals (163 sockets), 36 female and 97 male; mean age 58.6 years (range 19.6–94.1); sockets fitted between Nov 2018 and Nov 2022[16]
Measurements Used: Local rectification sizes measured as depth of carve or height of build-up between limb and socket surfaces; volume reduction (VR) computed from mean cross-sectional area differences at 10 sections between mid-patella tendon and distal tibia; use of landmarks (mid-patella, distal tibia) and principal axis for alignment; 3D mesh vertex-based metrics (98th percentile deviation)[16]
Study Design: Observational cohort study (retrospective analysis of CAD/CAM and 3D scan records)[16]
Key Findings: PTB sockets tended to have larger local rectifications while TSB sockets had greater gross volume reduction; socket designs exist on a PTB–TSB spectrum with many hybrids; significant correlations and probabilistic associations between certain rectification sizes (e.g., medial and lateral paratibial carves) were identified; Naïve Bayes models can predict likely rectification combinations and could inform CAD/CAM design templates to support clinician decision-making[16]
Quality Level: Moderate — observational cohort with a relatively large sample of 163 sockets/134 individuals and robust quantitative methods, but limited by retrospective CAD/CAM-only data, lack of soft-tissue palpation data and restricted generalisability[16]

Title: Current Issues Related to Anthropometry in Engineering[17]
Method: Reports manual anthropometry (anthrometer, sliding caliper, measuring tape) and body weight scales for dimensional measures, 3D scanning and 3D-model augmentation for detailed shape (pinnae/HRTF), low-cost depth cameras (Kinect) as alternatives, and force-plate-based measures to estimate segment masses and torso COM[17]
Product Type: Head-worn devices and wearables (including HRTF-related designs), hand-related products/tools, protective/sports/orthopaedic devices, and garment sizing implications[17]
Measurements Used: Hand dimensions (length, width, depth), waist and hip circumferences, pinnae anatomical dimensions, small-segment widths/depths (hands/feet), and segment masses/torso COM estimates from force-plate data[17]
Key Findings: Anthropometry-informed design improves product fit, comfort, and sustainability; conventional manual and some 3D methods have cost/efficiency limits; 3D models improve accuracy for complex shapes (pinnae); and up-to-date, population-specific reference data are necessary for effective ergonomic design[17]
Journal Source: Malaysian Journal of Engineering Research (source PDF)[17]
Quality Level: Moderate (review article summarising methods and issues; no primary experimental sample reported)[17]

Title: Shape Analysis of Prosthetic Socket Rectification Procedure for Transtibial Amputees[18]
Method: High-accuracy 3D surface scanning (EinScan Pro laser scanner) combined with an open-source shape analysis toolbox (AmpScan) including ICP alignment and cross-sectional slicing for extraction of geometric measures; post-processing and MATLAB analysis of extracted metrics (volume, perimeter, sagittal/coronal widths)[18]
Population: 44 transtibial residual limb casts (participants recruited from a single prosthetic facility in India); specific age range not mentioned in source[18]
Measurements Used: Geometric measures extracted: volume, perimeter, cross-sectional area, sagittal and coronal widths; 2 mm axial slicing; alignment to mid-patella reference; use of surface meshes (.stl)[18]
Study Design: Observational analytical study of paired unrectified and rectified casts using 3D scans (cross-sectional observational study with quantitative shape analysis)[18]
Key Findings: Rectification is concentrated at mid-patella and distal regions (notably 0-25% and distal end), with a mean local volume change ~6.02% (mid-patella to 25%); consistent sagittal-plane modifications; identification of five patient groups based on rectification patterns; results support creating data-driven socket design templates and training resources for clinicians[18]
Journal Source: MDPI journal (article PDF URL indicates MDPI publication) — full journal name not explicitly stated in source text.[18]
Quality Level: Moderate — observational study with a modest sample size (44 casts), validated scanning protocol, quantitative analysis but limited generalisability per authors' own limitations[18]

Title: THE PRODUCTION OF HYBRID PROSTHETIC SOCKETS THROUGH THE INTEGRATION OF 3D PRINTING AND CONVENTIONAL LAMINATION[19]
Method: 3D scanning of the residual limb using a structured-light scanner and orientation marks, CAD-based digital modification of the stump model, and additive manufacturing (FFF 3D printing of a PETG socket matrix) combined with conventional lamination (resin-saturated fabrics and silicone filling) for hybrid socket fabrication[19]
Population: Single-subject pilot (one 45-year-old male, transtibial/amputated below-knee, weight 65 kg, K-level/Functional Classification Level 4)[19]
Measurements Used: 3D scan-derived spatial resolution and depth parameters (resolution x/y 0.9 mm, depth resolution 1 mm) and landmark-based digital modifications: measurements and offsets relative to tibial condyles, distal end (e.g., 20 mm from distal end), added/removed mass in mm at specified regions for relief and pressure distribution (e.g., 2–4 mm modifications)[19]
Study Design: Pilot single-subject case study (experimental prototyping and mechanical testing)[19]
Key Findings: The hybrid 3D-printed PETG matrix with laminated outer layer maintained structural integrity under static and dynamic tests (no deviations at walking speeds tested) and was rated more comfortable by the user; hybrid design resisted failure modes seen in purely FFF sockets (supracondylar failures)[19]
Quality Level: Low (single-subject pilot study with limited generalizability)[19]

Title: Techniques for Measuring the Fluctuation of Residual Lower Limb Volume in Clinical Practices: A Systematic Review of the Past Four Decades[20]
Method: Systematic review of measurement methods including: water displacement, anthropometric circumference measurements using frustum/cylinder calculations[20], contact probes, optical/laser 3D scanning (silhouetting, fringe projection, handheld laser scanners)[20], imaging modalities (SXCT, MRI, ultrasound) and bioimpedance (multifrequency electrode-based impedance to estimate extracellular fluid volume)[20].
Product Type: Residual lower-limb prosthetic sockets (transtibial and transfemoral contexts)[20]
Population: Individuals with lower-limb amputation; majority of source studies involve transtibial amputees (36 studies) and fewer transfemoral (5 studies); some studies used able-bodied or model limbs[20].
Measurements Used: Segmental circumferences (tape measures) converted to volume via frustum/cylinder formulas[20]; radial surface geometry and volumes from optical/laser 3D scans[20]; in-socket extracellular fluid/volume changes from multifrequency bioimpedance with electrode placements[20].
Study Design: Systematic review of the literature covering 1975–2022; synthesized 39 peer-reviewed studies of varied designs (validation studies, reliability/test-retest studies, observational/experimental comparisons)[20].
Key Findings: Anthropometry (circumference) is simple and clinic-friendly but poorly correlates with true volume changes[20]; laser/optical 3D scanning provides high-precision surface geometry suitable for digital socket design and shows good reliability/validity in several studies[20]; bioimpedance is highly sensitive for real-time in-socket volume fluctuation measurement but mostly validated for transtibial limbs and measures change rather than absolute volume[20]. Recommendations: choose technique based on clinical phase and aim (anthropometry for early macroscopic monitoring; scanning/imaging for volumetric accuracy; bioimpedance/SXCT for sensitive change detection)[20].
Quality Level: Overall review-rated source studies as: 22 high-quality, 14 moderate-quality, 3 low-quality (the review used a 13-item adapted QUADAS-2 based quality scale)[20]

Title: A high precision laser scanning system for measuring shape and volume of transtibial amputee residual limbs: Design and validation[21]
Method: Uses an automated laser-line 3D scanning system (Micro-Epsilon scanCONTROL 2500-100) combined with a two-camera motion-capture based motion correction; automated linear and rotary stages to translate/rotate the scanner for repeatable scans[21]
Product Type: Transtibial prosthetic socket/residual limb measurement (prosthetic limb design implications)[21]
Population: Validation on a single unilateral transtibial amputee (60-year-old male); sample size = 1 (plus validation on geometric cylinder model)[21]
Measurements Used: Laser-line distance profiles (32 Hz, 640 points per line) to capture surface geometry; marker-based motion tracking (6-mm dots) for motion correction; derived cross-sectional diameters, surface area, and volume from meshed point clouds[21]
Study Design: Experimental validation study (system development and validation using physical cylinder model and single-subject human testing)[21]
Key Findings: The scanner achieved high spatial and volumetric accuracy (mean volumetric error 0.17% static; cylinder and human scans with low TEM and high ICC); motion-correction reduced dynamic scan errors; demonstrated repeatable residual limb volume measures and detection of short-term volume change (~4% increase after standing)[21]
Journal Source: PLOS ONE (article PDF hosted at journals.plos.org)[21]
Quality Level: Moderate — high technical validation on models (low measurement error, strong reliability metrics), but limited human sample size (n=1) reduces generalizability[21]

Title: A scoping review of digital fabrication techniques applied to prosthetics and orthotics: part 1 prostheses[22]
Method: Scoping review extracting methods across studies, focusing on digital anthropometry workflows: digital scanning of residual limbs, CAD-based modeling and rectification, and additive manufacture (CAD/CAM and AM) stages; systematic literature search and data extraction into tabulated fields including workflows and TRL[22]
Product Type: Prosthetic devices: lower-limb prosthetic sockets, prosthetic feet, upper-limb prosthetic hands and fingers[22]
Measurements Used: Residual limb dimensions (manual measurements and 3D scanning), anatomical scans used for CAD rectification; measurement techniques summarized as manual measurement, 3D scanning within AnatCADAM workflows[22]
Study Design: Scoping review (literature review) synthesizing peer-reviewed studies up to July 28, 2021[22]
Key Findings: Many studies use CAD/CAM or AnatCADAM workflows (3D scanning→CAD rectification→AM) but often lack documentation of postprocessing and rectification; evidence gaps include few long-term, large-scale trials and limited reporting on training and modification practices, limiting design translation[22]
Quality Level: Moderate (scoping review summarizing mostly low-to-moderate quality primary studies concentrated at TRL 3–4 with few higher-TRL trials)[22]

Title: A scoping review of digital fabrication techniques applied to orthosis fabrication[22]
Method: Scoping review extracting methods across studies, including digital anatomical capture (3D scanning), manual measurements, CAD-based rectification (including clinically informed CAD), finite element analysis for design optimization, pressure mapping and gait analysis for evaluation, and various additive manufacturing/CAD-CAM fabrication workflows[22]
Product Type: Orthoses (lower-limb orthoses: insoles, AFOs; upper-limb orthoses: wrist/hand orthoses and casts; spinal orthoses: TLSOs/collars)[22]
Measurements Used: Common measurements and techniques reported across included studies include plantar pressure mapping, CT-based geometry for FEA, 3D surface scans of anatomical regions, and standard clinical metrics for scoliosis such as Cobb angle, apical vertebral rotation and trunk listing[22]
Study Design: Scoping review of original research comprising experimental trials, randomized controlled trials, observational cohort studies, case studies, and technical evaluations (mixed study designs)[22]
Key Findings: Digital workflows (3D scanning + CAD rectification + AM/CAM) are increasingly used; strong evidence supports CAD/CAM for spinal braces and insoles, but gaps include limited long-term on-patient evaluation for many device types, incomplete reporting of rectification steps, and variability in materials and durability affecting fit and comfort recommendations[22]
Quality Level: Mixed: high-moderate for CAD/CAM in spinal orthotics and insoles (several RCTs and large cohort studies), but overall evidence is variable with many small, early-stage studies limiting generalizability[22]

Title: Utilizing Additive Manufacturing for Economical Prosthetic Limb Prototyping: A Guide from Regression Modelling[23]
Method: Manual anthropometric measurement (flexible measuring tape for ASIS to medial malleolus and acromion to olecranon) on 250 participants, statistical analysis with descriptive statistics and multivariate regression modelling to produce predictive equations, and CAD-based 3D prosthesis prototyping using SolidWorks for additive manufacturing[23]
Product Type: Lower-limb prosthetic (below-knee prosthetic) prototype intended for prosthetic limb design and additive manufacturing[23]
Population: 250 healthy young adults (male and female), ages 22–35 years[23]
Measurements Used: Linear segment measurements: total leg length (ASIS to medial malleolus) and elbow/upper arm length (acromion to olecranon) measured with flexible tape; RLL, LLL, REL, LEL recorded in cm[23]
Study Design: Observational descriptive study with multivariate regression modelling to develop predictive equations for limb length[23]
Key Findings: Developed a multivariate regression model with very high predictive accuracy (r=0.993, r²=0.986) allowing estimation of right leg length from left leg and elbow lengths; derived equation (RLL = 2.253 + 0.959 LLL + 0.054 LEL) and demonstrated translation to a 3D-printed lower-limb prosthetic prototype, recommending further validation across diverse populations[23]
Journal Source: Semantic Scholar entry for the article (full journal name not provided in source)[23]
Quality Level: Moderate quality: reasonable sample size (n=250) and clear methods with regression validation, but limited by single-population sampling (healthy young adults, Nigeria) and no clinical testing on amputee users[23]

Title: Relationship between Learning Environment Design and Musculoskeletal Disorders in Learners[24]
Method: Manual anthropometric data collection using stadiometer and tape measure, each measurement averaged over three trials, statistical analysis including means, SD, percentiles (5th,50th,95th), and match/mismatch calculations using one-way and two-way limits equations to compare body measurements with furniture dimensions[24]
Population: University students from Kumasi Technical University, Ghana; sample n=188 (108 males, 80 females); age 18–32, mean 22.86 years[24]
Measurements Used: Anthropometric measures: popliteal-to-floor height, elbow-to-seat height, thigh thickness, sitting height, buttock-to-popliteal length, buttock-to-knee length, elbow-to-elbow breadth, width of bitrochanter, subscapular height, sitting shoulder height, and stature; Design dimensions: seat height, backrest upper edge, seat width, seat depth, table length/width/height, backrest height, footrest[24]
Study Design: Observational cross-sectional anthropometric study with statistical analysis (descriptive percentiles and match/mismatch comparisons)[24]
Key Findings: High prevalence of mismatch between student anthropometry and classroom furniture: notably seat width, seat depth, backrest height/upper edge, and table height (up to 92.6–100% mismatch). Authors provide percentile-based recommended furniture dimensions to improve ergonomic fit and reduce MSD risk[24]
Journal Source: Semantics Scholar record / unspecified journal (source metadata)[24]
Quality Level: Moderate — cross-sectional study with reasonable sample size (n=188) and standard anthropometric methods; limited by single-site sampling and unspecified peer-reviewed journal details[24]

Title: A Workflow for Studying the Stump	6Socket Interface in Persons with Transtibial Amputation through 3D Thermographic Mapping[25]
Method: Integrated 2D thermal image acquisition and 3D surface scanning with spatial registration using 3D thermographic markers; Kinect-based 3D scanning with Skanect; thermal camera calibration and image-to-geometry registration in MeshLab; color-temperature mapping using MATLAB image processing and an ANN to map RGB to temperature[25]

Measurements Used: Thermal temperature matrices (240x320 pixels) mapped onto high-resolution 3D meshes (~16k vertices) using 3D thermographic markers; registration accuracy reported (median error 2.7 mm)[25]
Study Design: Method development and feasibility case study (experimental single-subject)[25]
Key Findings: Feasibility: successful integration of thermal and 3D data with median registration error 2.7 mm; identified hot spots post-walking useful to inform socket adjustments; protocol uses low-cost, widely available tools and markers and can support socket manufacturing decisions[25]

Title: Review and critique of current testing protocols for upper-limb prostheses: a call for standardization amidst rapid technological advancements[26]
Method: Systematic narrative review of task-based assessment protocols; extraction and analysis of methods used in identified tests including motion capture and eye-tracking (GaMA)[26], task-based object manipulation protocols such as AHAP using standardized object sets and rater scoring[26].
Population: Pediatric and adult prosthesis users as represented in reviewed studies; varied sample sizes across included tests (not summarized in source)[26]
Measurements Used: Measurement techniques include motion capture and eye-tracking for kinematics and gaze (GaMA)[26], inertial measurement units and pressure mats for movement/deviation metrics (PHAM)[26], and standardized object dimensions/counts for task scoring (BBT)[26].
Study Design: Narrative review of peer-reviewed assessment studies and protocols (summary and critique of 25 validated tests)[26]
Key Findings: Identified gaps: lack of standardized measures, limited integration of patient feedback in most tests[26]; recommendation for dual clinical/research testing streams to balance efficiency and comprehensiveness[26]; highlighted design-relevant factors affecting prosthesis use such as socket fit and comfort that influence adoption[26].
Journal Source: Frontiers in Robotics and AI (Front. Robot. AI)[26]
Quality Level: Moderate — peer-reviewed narrative review synthesizing many validated assessment studies; provides broad critique but does not present new primary anthropometric data[26]

Title: Functionality and Comfort Design of Lower-Limb Prosthetics: A Review[27]
Method: Discusses manual plaster casting, 3D scanning and digital modeling, CAD/CAM workflows for 3D printing, finite element analysis (FEA), and pressure-mapping/computer simulation methods for socket design and load distribution[27]
Product Type: Lower-limb prosthetic devices (transtibial/transtemporal sockets, transfemoral prostheses, prosthetic feet and knees)[27]
Population: Individuals with lower-limb amputations; specific cited studies include transtibial and transfemoral populations but source does not consistently list sample sizes or age ranges for all referenced papers[27]
Measurements Used: Residual limb shape and dimensions (3D surface geometry), socket–residual limb interface pressures/pressure mapping, stump–socket interface stress, and limb volume (to address volume fluctuations)[27]
Study Design: Systematic literature review (design synthesizing peer-reviewed studies)[27]
Key Findings: Highlights that anthropometric and anatomical capture methods (plaster casting, 3D scanning) combined with CAD/FEA and pressure-mapping inform socket design; design recommendations include adjustable sockets to accommodate volume changes and use of simulation/pressure data to optimize load distribution and comfort[27]
Quality Level: Moderate — systematic review summarizing many peer-reviewed studies (91 references), but level depends on quality of included studies rather than new primary data[27]

Title: Advances in the measurement of prosthetic socket interface mechanics: a review of technology, techniques, and a 20-year update[28]
Method: Narrative review of sensor and measurement methods including insertion of thin-film pressure sensors (force-sensitive resistors) between residual limb and socket, force transducer load-cells embedded in socket walls, capacitive sensors, fiber Bragg grating (fiber optic) sensors, fluid-filled (pneumatic) sensors, electronic skin (E-skin), benchtop testing and in-socket clinical measurements, and discussion of 3D-printed integrated sensor designs[28]
Product Type: Lower-limb and upper-limb prosthetic sockets (transtibial, transfemoral, transradial, transhumeral, shoulder disarticulation)[28]
Population: Aggregated literature across 87 articles covering participants with transtibial, transfemoral, transradial, transhumeral amputations and shoulder disarticulation; individual study sample sizes vary across included papers (not detailed in this review)[28]
Measurements Used: Interface mechanical measures: normal pressures (reported range 12.5–760 kPa), shear stresses (~45–78 kPa), force magnitudes, pressure distributions, and related metrics captured via sensor placement either between limb and liner or between liner and socket[28]
Study Design: Narrative review of experimental and clinical measurement studies (review synthesizing 87 articles covering benchtop experiments and in-socket clinical measurements)[28]
Key Findings: Sensor technologies can provide quantitative data to inform socket fabrication and assessment, but many experimental sensors lack clinical validation and ease-of-use; commercially available systems (e.g., Tekscan F-Socket) are commonly used despite accuracy limits, and larger, standardized clinical studies are needed to translate methods into practice[28]
Quality Level: Moderate — narrative review synthesizing 87 studies including benchtop and small clinical studies; highlights experimental methods but notes limited large-scale clinical validation across technologies[28]

Title: Low limb prostheses and complex human prosthetic interaction: A systematic literature review[29]
Method: Systematic literature review extracting methods reported across studies: manual/biopotential measurements (sEMG/iEMG), EEG-based BCI, IMU and environmental sensors (force plates, cameras, GRF), 3D motion capture (Vicon), and machine learning for interpretation and control[29]
Measurements Used: Inertial measurements (IMU: acceleration, angular rate), ground reaction force (GRF), motion capture kinematics (Vicon), sEMG/iEMG, EEG, pressure sensors, and encoder/current sensors for joint angles/power[29]
Study Design: Systematic literature review (review) summarising 194 selected articles[29]
Key Findings: Identified need for standardised design structure (HPI, sensing, electronics, control), gaps in energy management, and recommendation to integrate anthropometric/biomechanical sensing (IMU, GRF, motion capture) and ML-based interpretation for fit, ergonomics and control[29]
Journal Source: Frontiers in Robotics and AI (Front. Robot. AI)[29]
Quality Level: Moderate (systematic review summarising 194 articles; provides breadth but depends on included studies)[29]

Key Findings: The study reports substantial manufacturing cost reductions (~60%) and time savings (400 work hours per year) from using 3D technologies for custom-fitted prosthetic arm sockets[30]

Title: Ergonomic guidelines for the design interfaces of additive modules for manual wheelchairs: sagittal plane[31]
Method: Motion-capture using video markers (AruCo markers) with GoPro HERO7 and OpenCV-based proprietary software to extract 2D point clouds; alpha-shape contouring and averaging; post-processing in Rhinoceros/Grasshopper to standardise loops and define averaged hand-reach areas[31]
Population: Ten manual wheelchair users (N=10); participants chosen to reflect 50th-percentile anthropometric dimensions; similar age and physical condition (no detailed age range reported)[31]
Measurements Used: 2D positional measurements of hand marker (ID1) relative to wheelchair reference marker (ID0) in sagittal plane; extracted point clouds converted to contours (alpha-shape), averaged to define four reach areas; control points and confidence intervals reported; shoulder height measured experimentally[31]
Study Design: Experimental observational study with in-situ motion capture; repeated measures (three tests per participant) averaged to define reach areas (N=30)[31]
Key Findings: Defined four sagittal-plane hand-reach zones (AoC, AoA, AoR, AoP) with control points and confidence intervals to guide placement of accessory interfaces; recommend placing frequently-used or force-requiring controls within AoC/AoA and locating infrequent or low-force controls in AoR; provide point lists for plotting on wheelchair frames[31]
Quality Level: Moderate: peer-reviewed experimental study with clear methods and open-data availability but small sample size (N=10) limits generalisability[31]

Title: An Integrative Computational Design Workflow and Validation Methodology for 3D-Printed Personalized Orthopedic Devices: Case Study of a Wrist‑Hand Orthosis (WHO)[32]
Method: 3D surface scanning to capture limb point clouds, CAD processing and mesh cleaning/repair, parametric/visual-programming-based CAD customization (Grasshopper + Rhinoceros), and FEA for design validation and optimization; applied in a semi-automated workflow to generate 3D-printable orthosis geometry[32]
Population: Patients requiring immobilization for distal radial/ulnar and carpal fractures; specific sample size and age range not mentioned in source.[32]
Measurements Used: 3D surface point clouds with high-resolution laser scanning (50 μm nominal, 30 μm accuracy); manual reference linear and circumferential measurements (wrist-elbow distance, arm length, palm/wrist/elbow circumferences); mesh processing steps (noise removal, decimation, tessellation, hole repair) used to produce watertight STL for CAD[32]
Study Design: Methodology development and case study with prototype fabrication and multi-modal validation (observational/experimental case study)[32]
Key Findings: A parametric 3D scanning-to-CAD workflow produced a functional dual-material WHO that withstood mechanical loads in testing without failure; FEA guided design changes (added fastening band); dimensional accuracy showed substantial portions of surfaces within ±0.1 mm tolerances; materials showed no significant proinflammatory response in vitro—supporting feasibility of the workflow for personalized orthosis design[32]
Quality Level: Moderate: single case-study/method development with prototype fabrication and laboratory validation but without large user trials or clinical sample size; data available upon request supports transparency[32]

Title: Product Development of Assistive Technology for the Feet of a Person with Cerebral Palsy
Method: 3D scanning of a plaster mold; generation of 3D CAD model; additive manufacturing (Fused Deposition Modeling).

Title: Introduction to the Special Issue, Anthropometry in Design[33]
Method: Discussion of multiple anthropometric methods: manual/standard measurements and ranges, 3D/4D body scanning for surface capture[33], and multivariate/statistical techniques including PCA and Virtual Fit Test (VFT) using CAESAR data[33].
Product Type: Wearable products and furniture (including school furniture); general discussion applicable to prosthetic/assistive product design[33].
Population: Referenced datasets: ANSUR2 (6,068 US Army personnel: 4,082 males, 1,986 females) and CAESAR (≈5,000 civilian subjects aged 18–65)[33].
Measurements Used: General anthropometric measures: circumferences, segment lengths, body mass; datasets contain many specific measurements (e.g., ANSUR2 includes 93 measurements)[33].
Study Design: Editorial/overview introducing a special issue (literature overview and data-source discussion), not an original experimental study[33].
Key Findings: Highlights the value of 3D/4D scanning for capturing body surfaces in motion[33], recommends multivariate methods (PCA, VFT) for estimating accommodation in multivariate designs[33], and notes context-dependent fit tolerances including tight tolerance needs for prostheses[33].
Journal Source: Special issue introduction (repository.tudelft.nl) / editorial in the special issue 'Anthropometry in Design'[33]
Quality Level: Moderate (overview/editorial summarizing methods and datasets; useful for methods and theory but not primary empirical prosthetics studies)[33]

Title: Automated Design and Rapid Manufacturing of Low-Cost Customized Upper Limb Prostheses[38]

Key Findings: Key findings: Automated CAD-driven workflow based on 3D scans can generate customized upper-limb prostheses; printed sockets matched stump geometry in collision analyses; approach reduced design time to minutes and lowered costs, though clinical fitting and broader validation remain necessary[38]

Comparison of Traditional, MRI, and 3D Scanning Anthropometric Measurements in Hand Prosthesis Design[40]

Title: Design for All – Design for Disabled: How important is anthropometry?[42]

Product Type: Mobility and accessibility products / environments (assistive devices, wheelchairs, built-environment accessibility)[42]

Title: 3D Body Scan as Anthropometric Tool for Individualized Prosthetic Socks[43]
Method: Used a Vitronic VITUSSMART LC full 3D body scanner with custom scanning scenario and Anthroscan software configuration; manual tape measurements per ISO 7250 for validation; measurements extracted via software length and cross-sectional tools; statistical analysis included paired t-tests, MAD, TEM, CV, and reliability constant calculations[43]
Product Type: Prosthetic interface textile: individualized prosthetic socks / prosthetic stockings for upper-limb (arm) amputations[43]
Population: Eight adult volunteers (4 men, 4 women); participants were persons without mobility disorders; sample size = 8[43]
Measurements Used: Three longitudinal length measures and three circumferential measures per arm (total 12 locations); lengths measured between physical markers, circumferences via planar cross-sections in scanner software; markers placed to align manual and digital measures[43]

Journal Source: Autex Research Journal (article available at sciendo.com)[43]
Quality Level: Low — small sample (n=8) experimental validation; authors recommend larger sample (≥85) for stronger statistics[43]

Method: Manual anthropometric measurements with tailor tape (23 clothing-industry dimensions) and scaling of a reference biomechanical model, followed by a Python-implemented personalization algorithm that applies polynomial interpolation to morph the scaled model to subject-specific dimensions (mesh morphing/polynomial-based surface personalization)[46]
Product Type: Personal protective equipment / clothing patterns (PPE) and general virtual human body models applicable to PPE, orthopedic tools, and vehicle safety systems[46]

Quality Level: Moderate — moderate sample size across varied age groups (N=220), observational measurement study with algorithm implementation but limited to specific populations and lacking broader external validation[46]
